country.comment: Single-country study in Costa Rica examining a water conflict between the communities of Atenas (Atenas canton) and Tacares (Grecia canton) in Alajuela province.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title and Resumen/Abstract; PDF p. 3, Section 1; PDF p. 8, Map 1

effect_estimate.comment: Purely qualitative case study reconstructing a ~7-8 year socio-environmental conflict (2012-2019) over water sources; the 60% rationing figure in Atenas (2014) is cited background context from a secondary news report (Fornaguera 2014), with no primary quantitative effect estimate.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Unplanned real-estate growth without municipal land-use/regulatory plans left Atenas canton with severe water shortages (60% of its 25,460 residents facing daily rationing in 2014, cited from secondary news), prompting the national water utility (AyA) in December 2012 to launch a top-down 2,800-million-colones water transfer project from Parque Los Chorros in neighboring Tacares without prior community consultation. Tacares residents mobilized and used legal remedies (a constitutional writ of amparo and annulment of environmental viability) that halted the project and forced state-led negotiation (direct negotiation with a community Technical Negotiating Commission in 2013–2014 and subsequent facilitation by the Ombudsman, Defensoría de los Habitantes) as well as creation of AyA's Social Management and Citizen Participation Unit in 2014. However, negotiations reproduced power asymmetries (compelling residents to hire technical/legal experts to adopt technical framing), a preliminary agreement failed community assembly ratification, facilitated talks reached no consensus, and after roughly seven to eight years of delay AyA completed the project in 2019 as originally designed without incorporating negotiated community alternatives; institutional actors promoted participation only reactively once conflict escalated and obstructed project execution.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Resumen/Abstract; PDF p. 3, Section 1; PDF pp. 10-12, Section 3; PDF pp. 14-15, Section 4

mechanism_certainty.comment: Rated 2 (mechanism directly observed; maximum allowed under the CASP Qualitative Checklist ceiling of 2) because primary interviews with community and institutional actors and official minutes directly document how top-down project imposition, judicial remedies (amparo and environmental viability annulment), and institutional negotiation/facilitation processes operated on water project delay and ultimate execution.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 3-4, Section 1; PDF pp. 10-12, Section 3; PDF pp. 14-15, Section 4

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines lack of land-use/urban regulatory planning (planning), top-down exclusion and reactive community negotiation/consultation mechanisms (participation), constitutional amparo litigation and annulment of environmental viability halting works (judicial_review), Ombudsman facilitation by the Defensoría de los Habitantes (administrative_review), multi-actor coordination/confrontation across AyA, local municipalities, and the Tacares ASADA (political_coordination), and prolonged institutional/construction delays from 2012 to 2019 (delay); land tenure issues in the park (tenure) are also noted in the 2014 preliminary agreement.
mechanism_flags.value: ELIGIBILITY, BURDEN, DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, ENFORCEMENT, planning, tenure, delay, participation, administrative_review, judicial_review, political_coordination
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 2-3, Section 1; PDF pp. 8-13, Section 3, Figure 1; PDF pp. 14-15, Section 4

outcome_flags.comment: Analyzes community water access and supply security for Atenas and Tacares (water_access), permanent access vs. daily rationing (service_continuity), water capture/transfer flow volume (service_quantity), and multi-year paralysis/delay of water supply infrastructure works from 2012 to 2019 (delay).
outcome_flags.where_found: PDF p. 1, Resumen/Abstract; PDF p. 3, Section 1; PDF pp. 10, 12, Section 3; PDF p. 14, Section 4
